title: The boycott
hook: For about three years, his whole clan was shut out: no trade, no marriage, barely any food.

screens.text: **For about three years, his whole clan was shut out.** No trade. No marriage. Barely any food. And relatives who didn't share his faith went through it with him.
**A pact against a clan.** Quraysh swore an agreement against his clan, Banu Hashim, and Banu al-Muttalib: no marrying them and no trading with them until they handed him over [Bukhari 1590].
bubbles: Years later, during Hajj, he named the very place where that pact had been sworn [Bukhari 1590].

screens.situation: You're there. You belong to his clan, but you aren't Muslim. Because of the pact, your family will go hungry too. Handing him over would end it. What do you do?

options.feedback: That's what his clan did, Muslims and non-Muslims alike. They stayed with him through years of hunger.

options.text: Hand him over so the rest of the clan can eat
options.feedback: Not quite. His clan refused, even those who didn't share his faith. Family loyalty held.

options.text: Quietly leave the clan and join Quraysh
options.feedback: Not quite. Most of his clan stayed together, under his uncle Abu Talib's protection.

screens.text: **Into the valley.** Abu Talib led the clan, Muslims and non-Muslims alike, into a valley to keep him safe, the early biographers say [Qalam ep. 48]. It lasted about three years, with severe hunger [Qalam ep. 48; Yaqeen].
About three years, and how it ended.

events.title: The pact
events.text: Quraysh swear: no marriage or trade with his clan until they hand him over [Bukhari 1590].

events.title: Into the valley
events.text: Abu Talib leads the whole clan there to protect him, the early biographers say [Qalam ep. 48].

events.title: Hunger
events.text: Food is scarce and the hardship is severe [Qalam ep. 48; Yaqeen].

events.title: Consciences speak
events.text: Some Makkans campaign against the boycott, and it ends [Qalam ep. 50].

events.title: The Year of Sorrow
events.text: Soon after, he loses Khadijah and Abu Talib [Bukhari 3896; IslamQA 11575].

screens.text: **Consciences wake up.** In the end, some Makkans with a conscience campaigned against the boycott, and it was brought to an end, the early biographers say [Qalam ep. 50].
bubbles: Not everyone in Makkah agreed with the cruelty. Some spoke up, even against their own leaders.

screens.prompt: Why did relatives who weren't Muslim go hungry alongside him?

options.text: Family loyalty: they wouldn't hand over one of their own
options.feedback: Right. They didn't share his faith, but they wouldn't abandon him. Loyalty like that deserves honour.
Not quite. Many of them weren't Muslim. They stood by him because he was family.

options.text: Quraysh forced them into the valley
options.feedback: Not quite. Abu Talib led them there to protect him. They chose to stay together.

screens.text: **Unexpected loyalty.** Relatives who didn't share his faith went hungry for him. Your family may surprise you too: a parent who drives you to the masjid, a cousin who defends you. Notice it, and honour it.
bubbles: And for the Muslims in the valley, three years of **sabr** (patient endurance) ended in relief.

screens.situation: Destiny's dad still doesn't understand why she became Muslim. But when a neighbour made a nasty comment about her faith, her dad told him firmly to back off.

options.text: Thank her dad and tell him how much it meant
options.feedback: Yes. Loyalty across faiths is precious. His clan stood by the Prophet ﷺ, and he never forgot it.

options.text: Assume he only did it out of pride
options.feedback: Not quite. Give him credit. Standing up for her was love, whatever he thinks of her faith.

options.text: Say nothing; he isn't Muslim, so it doesn't count
options.feedback: Not quite. Loyalty from family of another faith counts, and it deserves thanks.

chips: Why did Quraysh boycott his clan?
My non-Muslim family stood up for me. How do I thank them?

steps: Think of a family member who isn't Muslim and has stood by you
Thank them today, with words or a small favour

screens.text: Family who didn't share his faith went hungry beside him. Loyalty from loved ones of another faith is something to honour.
Next episode: in one year, he loses the wife who believed him first and the uncle who shielded him.

check.prompt: What did the pact against his clan forbid?

options.text: Marrying them or trading with them
options.feedback: Right. Until they handed him over, which they refused to do [Bukhari 1590].
Not quite. It cut them off from marriage and trade, to starve them into handing him over [Bukhari 1590].

check.prompt: Who went into the valley with him?

options.text: His clan, Muslims and non-Muslims alike
options.feedback: Right. Abu Talib led them there to protect him, the early biographers say.
Not quite. Relatives who weren't Muslim went too, out of family loyalty.

aiContext:
**Lesson facts**
- Quraysh swore a pact against Banu Hashim and Banu al-Muttalib: no marriage or trade with them until they handed him over [Bukhari 1590].
- Abu Talib took the clan, Muslims and non-Muslims alike, into a valley (Shi'b Abi Talib) to protect him [Qalam ep. 48]. Single present-day source: say "the early biographers say".
- It lasted about three years, with severe hunger [Qalam ep. 48; Yaqeen].
- It ended when some Makkans with a conscience campaigned against it [Qalam ep. 50]. Single source: keep it cautious.

**Likely questions**
- *"Is it true termites ate the boycott document, except Allah's name?"* It's a popular story, but its chain hasn't been verified for this track, so it's left out. Don't tell it as fact. (scholar question Q43)
- *"Did Abu Talib become Muslim?"* He never accepted Islam, yet he protected the Prophet ﷺ all his life, and the Prophet ﷺ loved him. The next episode covers his death. Questions about his afterlife: there are sahih texts, the guide doesn't deny them or speculate, Allah alone judges, and the imam is offered. (scholar question Q42)
- *"Who exactly was in the valley?"* His clan, Banu Hashim, with Banu al-Muttalib, Muslims and non-Muslims alike [Bukhari 1590; Qalam ep. 48]. Keep to that.
- *"My non-Muslim family stood up for me."* Encourage thanks and closeness; Day 65 and Day 14.

**Escalate:** the afterlife of Abu Talib or of the convert's own relatives (Q42, Q23); unsafe family situations (safety rule).

**Don't**
- Don't tell the termite story.
- Don't describe the hunger in graphic detail.
- Don't suggest a convert's family loves them less for not being Muslim.
- Don't picture the Prophet ﷺ.
